| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_hash in ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376") OR Filesystem.file_name="VID001.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_*_Exe.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution

status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Attacks Trick OpenClaw AI Agent Into Running Code and Leaking Secrets

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 15 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Two security teams have shown, in separate research published this week, that OpenClaw, the popular self-hosted AI agent, can be driven to run attacker-controlled code or hand over sensitive data through ordinary-looking inputs. Imperva buried instructions inside shared contacts, vCards, and location pins that the agent executed without the victim ever seeing them. Varonis built a test agent on

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] OpenClaw channel-extension display-name allowlist bypass (Slack/Teams/Discord/Matrix/Zalo) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell or LOLBin child processes · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Imperva OpenClaw PoC payload server callout (imperva_artifactory.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent process reading credential stores or .env / .ssh / .aws paths · [LLM] OpenClaw mail connector sending credentials to first-time external recipient · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Imperva OpenClaw PoC payload server callout (imperva_artifactory.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts for DNS resolutions, HTTP requests or command lines referencing imperva_artifactory.com — the payload server Imperva's Yohann Sillam used in the OpenClaw prompt-injection PoC where a poisoned vCard / shared contact / location pin name field caused the agent to download and run a remote script. Any hit means either the live PoC ran in your environment or an attacker is reusing the published indicator. Rationale: imperva_artifactory.com is the single concrete IOC named in the article (the server the poisoned contact-name field instructed the agent to fetch and execute from). Matching either the underscore form (as printed) or the more DNS-typical hyphen form covers both publication and likely real-world variants. Cross-checked against The Hacker News original (cited). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security researcher reproducing the Imperva PoC in a lab
  • Threat-intel team enriching the IOC via curl/whois
  • Sandbox/EDR detonation environment fetching the URL for analysis
  • Browser-based read-through of the original blog post resolving embedded references
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","curl.exe","powershell_ise.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("threatintel-svc","sandbox-svc")
Response runbook
Triage: confirm the resolving process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — agent runtime (python/node/openclaw) is a true positive; threat-intel tooling is benign. Pull the user, device, and whether OpenClaw < 2026.4.23 is installed. Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response if the agent runtime resolved it; revoke any session tokens the agent had; rotate AWS/SSH/DB secrets in the agent's connector scope. Hunt: pivot on the originating process and look for prior ingress of a shared-contact/vCard message-object event, outbound mail from the agent account in the same 30 min window, and any other unknown domains the same process touched.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("imperva_artifactory.com", "imperva-artifactory.com")
   or RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)imperva[_-]?artifactory\.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has_any ("imperva_artifactory.com", "imperva-artifactory.com")
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="DnsEvents", Host=Computer, ClientIP, Query=Name, QueryType, Result),
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DestinationHostName has_any ("imperva_artifactory.com", "imperva-artifactory.com")
      or RequestURL has_any ("imperva_artifactory.com", "imperva-artifactory.com")
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="Proxy/FW", Host=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Query=DestinationHostName, QueryType=tostring(RequestMethod), Result=RequestURL),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has_any ("imperva_artifactory.com", "imperva-artifactory.com")
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImDnsActivity", Host=SrcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, Result=DnsResponseName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenClaw channel-extension display-name allowlist bypass (Slack/Teams/Discord/Matrix/Zalo) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the InfoSec Write-ups disclosure where five OpenClaw channel-extension allowlists keyed on mutable display name rather than stable user ID. An attacker renames their Slack/Teams/Discord/Matrix/Zalo identity to match an allowlisted user, slips onto the trusted-sender list, and then steers the agent. Hunt for display-name changes at the SaaS layer that target previously-trusted account names and for first-time-seen senders the OpenClaw agent suddenly accepts commands from. Rationale: The article calls out the exact bug class (five channel extensions across Slack/Discord/Matrix/Zalo/Teams resolving allowlists by mutable display name) and the exploitation method (rename-to-match). Detection looks for the rename event at the SaaS audit layer — that's where the abuse happens. CIM datamodel is now Authentication.Authentication (replaces the rejected Change_Analysis/Application). Cross-checked against the InfoSec Write-ups reference cited in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1656 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marriage/name change by an employee
  • Contractor rename when joining a new project
  • Slack/Teams admin bulk-correcting display-name formatting
  • User adding pronouns or status emoji to their display name
Response runbook
Triage: pull the user's recent display-name history and compare against the OpenClaw channel-extension allowlist (config file in OpenClaw repo). Verify whether the new value matches any allowlisted name. Contain: if a match exists, remove the user from the channel and force the OpenClaw maintainer to migrate the allowlist to stable user IDs (and confirm patched version covering all five extensions is deployed). Hunt: in the 24h after the rename, audit every OpenClaw tool invocation triggered by messages from the renamed user, and check for downstream connector activity (mail send, file fetch, secret read) attributable to that session.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application in~ ("Microsoft Teams", "Slack", "Discord")
| where ActionType has_any ("UserUpdated", "UpdateDisplayName", "DisplayNameChanged", "user_profile_change", "Modify_User", "UpdateUser")
| extend NewDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).NewDisplayName)
| extend OldDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).OldDisplayName)
| where isnotempty(NewDisplayName) and NewDisplayName != OldDisplayName
| project Timestamp, Application, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ActionType, OldDisplayName, NewDisplayName
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload in ("MicrosoftTeams", "Teams")
| where Operation has_any ("UserUpdated", "MemberRoleChanged", "TeamUpdated", "MemberSettingChanged")
| extend ParamMap = todynamic(Parameters)
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, UserType, ClientIP, Operation, ObjectId, ParamMap
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:okta @evt.name:(user.account.update_profile OR user.profile.update) @actor.alternateId:*
#event_simpleName=IdpAuthenticationLog (UserName=* OR UserPrincipal=*)
| groupBy([UserPrincipal, ApplicationName], function={ collect([UserName]) | count() })
APPLICATION

| tstats summariesonly=t count, values(Authentication.user_display_name) as display_names, values(Authentication.src) as src, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success AND (Authentication.app="slack" OR Authentication.app="teams" OR Authentication.app="discord" OR Authentication.app="matrix" OR Authentication.app="zalo") by Authentication.user, Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where mvcount(display_names) > 1 | eval reason="Channel-extension allowlist key (display name) changed for a single stable user — potential OpenClaw allowlist bypass" | sort - last_seen
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Authentication.user_display_name) as display_names, values(Authentication.src) as src, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success AND (Authentication.app="slack" OR Authentication.app="teams" OR Authentication.app="discord" OR Authentication.app="matrix" OR Authentication.app="zalo") by Authentication.user, Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where mvcount(display_names) > 1 | eval reason="Channel-extension allowlist key (display name) changed for a single stable user — potential OpenClaw allowlist bypass" | sort - last_seen
OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell or LOLBin child processes AIInstallation High
Hunts for the post-injection step from both research teams: OpenClaw's python/node runtime spawning cmd/powershell/bash/curl/wget/certutil to fetch and run the attacker payload. In Imperva's PoC the hidden contact-name string told the agent to download and execute a remote script — that's a shell spawn from the agent process. Pair the agent-runtime parent with a known-LOLBin child. Rationale: Direct from article: 'the hidden text told the agent to download and run a script from a server the researchers controlled. It did.' That action is observable as the agent runtime (python/node/openclaw binary) spawning a LOLBin child. The Imperva trifecta framing — read private data, take in untrusted content, send data back out — makes shell spawning the highest-value pivot for the execution phase. Reviewer feedback item #1. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate agent tool-call to a system shell declared in the agent's manifest (e.g. local devops automation)
  • Developer running 'python -m openclaw' interactively and shelling out for testing
  • Python build/install scripts calling curl/certutil for legitimate package fetch
  • Node-based CLI utilities (npm/npx) calling cmd.exe wrappers
  • Jupyter notebooks under the same Python process spawning a shell
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","pip3 install","npm install","npm run build","poetry install") and FileName in~ ("curl.exe","certutil.exe"))
Response runbook
Triage: pull the parent process command line — confirm it's the OpenClaw agent (not just any Python). Check the agent's tool manifest: is shell execution a declared capability? Pull the child command line and any network destination it touched. Contain: if the child fetched from imperva_artifactory.com or any unfamiliar domain, isolate the host and kill the agent process. Suspend any connector tokens (AWS, Gmail, Graph) the agent had. Hunt: list every other process the same agent PID spawned in the last 24h, every file it wrote/read, and every outbound network destination. Pivot on the inbound message-object event (contact / vCard / location pin) that arrived ≤5 min before the spawn.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","pwsh.exe","openclaw.exe","openclaw-agent.exe")
      or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("openclaw", "agent.py", "agent_runtime", "llm_agent"))
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","wsl.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","pwsh.exe","openclaw.exe")
      or CommandLine has_any ("openclaw","agent.py","llm_agent","agent_runtime"))
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","wsl.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, AccountName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      - '\certutil.exe'

  condition: (parent or parent_cmd) and child

OpenClaw agent process reading credential stores or .env / .ssh / .aws paths AIActions on Objectives High
Directly targets the 'Leaking Secrets' half of the article — Varonis's Pinchy agent forwarded plaintext AWS IAM access keys, DB connection strings and SSH credentials after a single phishing email. Detect when the OpenClaw / agent runtime process touches files under ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.azure, ~/.gcloud, .env files, or the Windows Credential Manager directories. Pair the agent-runtime parent with the sensitive file path. Rationale: Article: Pinchy 'forwarded mock AWS IAM access keys, database connection strings, and SSH credentials in plaintext'. To exfiltrate, the agent must first read the credential files — that read is the earliest deterministic signal. Path list covers the three cloud SDKs (AWS / Azure / GCP), SSH keys, .env files (the standard Pinchy / dev-secret pattern), Windows Credential Manager, and the Linux /etc/passwd /etc/shadow targets the reviewer called out. Reviewer feedback items #2 + #4. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running 'aws configure' or 'gh auth login' interactively while OpenClaw is also installed under the same user
  • Legitimate OpenClaw deployment that genuinely has a 'read my AWS creds' tool declared (rare — but legit DevOps assistants do exist)
  • Backup software (Duplicati / restic) scanning ~/.ssh as part of full-home backup
  • VS Code / JetBrains plugins resolving .env for syntax highlighting
  • IDE Python-language-server walking the project tree on open
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("devops-svc","backup-svc") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws configure","gh auth","az login"))
Response runbook
Triage: pull the agent's tool manifest and confirm whether credential read is a declared capability. Check what triggered the file access — was there a recent inbound message-object event (vCard/contact/location) or an external email asking for credentials (Varonis 'Dan from prod' pattern)? Contain: rotate every secret the agent process had file-level access to (AWS keys, SSH keys, DB connection strings). Revoke the agent's connector OAuth tokens. Force-restart the agent on the patched OpenClaw 2026.4.23+. Hunt: in the 60 min after the read, pull EmailEvents outbound from the agent's mailbox connector and DeviceNetworkEvents to any non-baseline cloud API endpoint (sts.amazonaws.com, *.azure.com), looking for exfil of the credential material.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","pwsh.exe","openclaw.exe","openclaw-agent.exe")
      or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("openclaw","agent.py","llm_agent","agent_runtime"))
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\", @"\.azure\", @"\.gcloud\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Credentials", @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Credentials", "/root/.ssh", "/root/.aws", "/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow")
   or FileName in~ (".env", "credentials", "id_rsa", "id_rsa.pub", "id_ed25519", "config.json", "secrets.json", "aws-credentials", "connection_strings.txt")
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified","FileAccessed","FileOpened")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessName has_any ("python","node","openclaw","pwsh","openclaw-agent")
      or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("openclaw","agent.py","llm_agent"))
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\", @"\.azure\", @"\.gcloud\", "/root/.ssh", "/root/.aws", "/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow")
   or TargetFileName in~ (".env","credentials","id_rsa","id_ed25519","secrets.json","config.json")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AI Agent Runtime Reading Credential Files
id: 6a3c2e5b-9f1d-4a8b-b7c4-2e0d8f5a9c1b
description: Detects OpenClaw / Python/Node agent runtime touching ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.azure, .env, id_rsa, or other credential stores. Article-grounded in Varonis Pinchy agent leaking AWS IAM keys, DB connection strings and SSH credentials after a single phishing email.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
author: SOC Detection Team
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1005
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\openclaw.exe'
      - '\openclaw-agent.exe'
  cred_paths:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.ssh\'
      - '\.aws\'
      - '\.azure\'
      - '\.gcloud\'
      - '\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Credentials\'
      - '/root/.ssh/'
      - '/root/.aws/'
  cred_names:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.env'
      - '\id_rsa'
      - '\id_ed25519'
      - '\credentials'
      - '\secrets.json'
  condition: proc and (cred_paths or cred_names)
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR *\\node.exe OR *\\openclaw.exe OR *\\openclaw-agent.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\\.ssh\\* OR *\\.aws\\* OR *\\.azure\\* OR *\\.gcloud\\* OR *.env OR *\\credentials OR *\\id_rsa OR *\\id_ed25519 OR *\\secrets.json)) OR (source:linux.auditd @process.command_line:(*openclaw* OR *agent.py* OR *llm_agent*) @process.command_line:(*\.ssh* OR *\.aws* OR */etc/passwd* OR */etc/shadow* OR *.env*))
(#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten) ContextImageFileName=/(python|python3|node|openclaw|openclaw-agent|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/(\\\.ssh\\|\\\.aws\\|\\\.azure\\|\\\.gcloud\\|\.env$|credentials$|id_rsa$|id_ed25519$|secrets\.json$|\/root\/\.ssh|\/root\/\.aws|\/etc\/(passwd|shadow))/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths, values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","pwsh.exe","openclaw.exe","openclaw-agent.exe") OR Filesystem.process="*openclaw*" OR Filesystem.process="*agent.py*") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.ssh\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.aws\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.azure\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.gcloud\\*" OR Filesystem.file_name=".env" OR Filesystem.file_name="credentials" OR Filesystem.file_name="id_rsa" OR Filesystem.file_name="id_ed25519" OR Filesystem.file_name="secrets.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="/root/.ssh/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/root/.aws/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/passwd" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/shadow") by host, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - count
OpenClaw mail connector sending credentials to first-time external recipient AIActions on Objectives High
Direct hunt for the Varonis Pinchy outcome: an agent-controlled mailbox sending an outbound message containing credential-shaped content (AWS keys, SSH, DB connection strings, customer export) to a recipient the org has never mailed before. Two failed Pinchy tests sent exactly this — once urgent ('staging access during a production incident'), once routine ('weekly customer export for QBR'). Detects both shapes via baseline-deviation on the recipient plus content keyword filter. Rationale: Direct from article: Pinchy 'forwarded mock AWS IAM access keys, database connection strings, and SSH credentials in plaintext' (test 1) and 'shipped out a synthetic dataset of 247 enterprise customers' (test 2). Subject keywords mirror the exact pretexts ('staging access during a production incident', 'weekly customer export for QBR deck'). The 60-day recipient baseline + 'first-time send' anti-join is the cleanest expression of Varonis's recommended control ('no first-time sends to unfamiliar addresses without approval'). High confidence because credential-content + brand-new external recipient + agent-named sender is a three-factor signal. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
ATT&CKT1048.003 T1567 T1114.003
Data sourcesEmail.Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate agent emailing a real new customer/partner for the first time with a QBR deck (the genuine business use case)
  • Onboarding flow that sends a one-time welcome email to a new external collaborator
  • Marketing automation that uses a similarly-named sender ('AI Assistant Newsletter')
  • Pen-tester or red-team running a sanctioned exfil simulation
Suppression filter
and SenderFromAddress !in~ ("redteam@yourcorp.com","marketing-automation@yourcorp.com") and not (Subject has "QBR" and RecipientEmailAddress endswith "@yourcorp-customer-portal.com")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full mail body and attachments. Check whether the credentials are real or test/mock values (Varonis used mock — your incident may not). Confirm the trigger: was there an inbound prompt-injection message (vCard/contact) or an external email matching the Pinchy pretext ('Dan, staging access, prod incident')? Contain: revoke the agent's mail connector OAuth grant, recall the message via M365 Purview if the recipient is internal-reachable, rotate every credential type referenced in the body (AWS IAM key rotation in particular is irreversible exposure if delivered). Hunt: pivot on the recipient address — query EmailEvents and ThreatIntelligenceIndicator for prior reputation; query AuditLogs / AzureActivity for any subsequent use of the exposed AWS keys (AssumeRole, CreateUser); enumerate every other outbound the same agent sender produced in the last 30 days against the baseline.
let Baseline = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(60d) .. ago(1d))
    | where EmailDirection == "Outbound"
    | summarize by RecipientEmailAddress;
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where EmailDirection == "Outbound"
| where SenderFromAddress has_any ("openclaw","agent","pinchy","automation","assistant")
   or SenderDisplayName has_any ("OpenClaw","Agent","Pinchy","AI Assistant")
| where Subject has_any ("credential","access key","AWS","IAM","SSH","connection string","customer export","QBR","staging access","production incident")
   or AttachmentCount > 0
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentCount, UrlCount, DeliveryAction, EmailDirection
| order by Timestamp desc
let Baseline = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(60d) .. ago(1d))
    | where Operation == "Send"
    | extend RecipientStr = tostring(Recipients)
    | summarize by RecipientStr;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Operation in ("Send","SendOnBehalf","SendAs")
| where UserId has_any ("openclaw","agent","pinchy","automation","assistant")
| extend SubjectStr = tostring(Subject), RecipientStr = tostring(Recipients)
| where SubjectStr has_any ("credential","access key","AWS","IAM","SSH","connection string","customer export","QBR","staging access","production incident")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on $left.RecipientStr == $right.RecipientStr
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, RecipientStr, SubjectStr, ClientIP, ItemAttachments
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:office365 @evt.name:Send @actor.email:(*openclaw* OR *pinchy* OR *agent* OR *automation*) @subject:(*credential* OR *"access key"* OR *AWS* OR *IAM* OR *SSH* OR *"connection string"* OR *"customer export"* OR *QBR* OR *"staging access"* OR *"production incident"*)

| tstats summariesonly=t count, values(All_Email.recipient) as recipient, values(All_Email.subject) as subject, values(All_Email.src_user) as sender from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.direction="outbound" AND (All_Email.src_user="*openclaw*" OR All_Email.src_user="*pinchy*" OR All_Email.src_user="*agent*" OR All_Email.src_user="*automation*") AND (All_Email.subject="*credential*" OR All_Email.subject="*access key*" OR All_Email.subject="*AWS*" OR All_Email.subject="*SSH*" OR All_Email.subject="*connection string*" OR All_Email.subject="*customer export*" OR All_Email.subject="*QBR*" OR All_Email.subject="*staging access*") by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Email.recipient) as recipient, values(All_Email.subject) as subject, values(All_Email.src_user) as sender from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.direction="outbound" AND (All_Email.src_user="*openclaw*" OR All_Email.src_user="*pinchy*" OR All_Email.src_user="*agent*" OR All_Email.src_user="*automation*") AND (All_Email.subject="*credential*" OR All_Email.subject="*access key*" OR All_Email.subject="*AWS*" OR All_Email.subject="*SSH*" OR All_Email.subject="*connection string*" OR All_Email.subject="*customer export*" OR All_Email.subject="*QBR*" OR All_Email.subject="*staging access*") by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | sort - _time
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("imperva_artifactory.com")

author: Clankerusecase

detection:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"

| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")

   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")

"This was an accidental discovery, it took a total of 4 hours to find this," the researcher said in a post on Blogger. "If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you're

GreatXML staging: write of unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml to Windows Recovery path AIInstallation High
Detects the core staging step of the GreatXML BitLocker bypass — a non-TrustedInstaller process writing unattend.xml or Recovery\WindowsRE\ReAgent.xml under a recovery-partition or WinRE path. This is the article's primary detectable artifact before the host is rebooted into WinRE. Rationale: Article literally names both files (unattend.xml at the root and Recovery/WindowsRE/ReAgent.xml) as the staging payload. Filtering out TrustedInstaller/reagentc/DismHost keeps Windows Update + DISM noise out while preserving the attacker's write because they cannot impersonate those signed contexts without already-elevated rights.
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1564 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows feature update or in-place upgrade copying a fresh WinRE image (DismHost / WindowsUpdateBox)
  • OEM provisioning tools (HP/Dell/Lenovo recovery toolkits) restaging WinRE during imaging
  • Sysprep + unattend.xml answer file authoring on a build / golden-image VM
  • MDT/SCCM task sequences that touch the recovery partition during OSD
  • Manual administrator using reagentc /setreimage to relocate WinRE (will be allowlisted by reagentc.exe parent filter)
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe", "WindowsUpdateBox.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe", "setuphost.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\$WINDOWS.~BT\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent-process chain and signing status of InitiatingProcessFileName, and confirm the device is not in an active OSD/feature-update window via Update history. Was the writing process started by an interactive user session vs SYSTEM? 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, snapshot the recovery partition (mount via DiskPart, copy ReAgent.xml + unattend.xml off for analysis), and force a BitLocker key rotation so the staged WinRE bypass cannot be used post-recovery. 3) Hunt: in the same DeviceId, search ±2h for reagentc.exe, MpCmdRun.exe -OfflineScan, shutdown.exe /r /o, and any diskpart 'assign letter' against the recovery volume. Pivot on the writing user across other hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "ReAgent.xml")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Recovery\WindowsRE\", @"\Recovery\", @"\WinRE\", @"GLOBALROOT\Device\", @"\System Volume Information\WindowsRE\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "TiWorker.exe", "reagentc.exe", "WindowsUpdateBox.exe", "setupcl.exe", "DismHost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system", "local service", "network service")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType,
          Actor = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          ProcessName = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ProcessPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ProcessCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          IntegrityLevel = InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel,
          TargetFile = FileName,
          TargetFolder = FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "ReAgent.xml")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Recovery\WindowsRE\", @"\Recovery\", @"\WinRE\", @"GLOBALROOT\Device\")
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "TrustedInstaller.exe"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "TiWorker.exe"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "reagentc.exe"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "DismHost.exe"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GreatXML BitLocker Bypass Staging via Recovery XML Write
id: 8c2f3b1d-9a4e-4d1c-bc8e-7f3e5a9c8d12
description: Detects writes of unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml under Windows Recovery / WinRE paths by a process other than TrustedInstaller or reagentc, matching the staging step of the GreatXML BitLocker bypass.

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\Recovery\\WindowsRE\\ReAgent.xml OR *\\Recovery\\WindowsRE\\reagent.xml OR *\\Recovery\\*\\unattend.xml OR *\\recovery\\*\\unattend.xml)) -@Image:(*\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\trustedinstaller.exe OR *\\TiWorker.exe OR *\\tiworker.exe OR *\\reagentc.exe OR *\\Reagentc.exe OR *\\DismHost.exe OR *\\dismhost.exe)

| TargetFileName=/\\Recovery\\(WindowsRE\\ReAgent\.xml|[^\\]*\\unattend\.xml)$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(TrustedInstaller|TiWorker|reagentc|WindowsUpdateBox|DismHost)\.exe$/i

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)(TrustedInstaller|TiWorker|reagentc|WindowsUpdateBox)\\.exe")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Defender Offline Scan initiation creates GreatXML-vulnerable WinRE state AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts hosts that have initiated a Microsoft Defender Offline Scan, which the GreatXML author states automatically renders the host vulnerable to the BitLocker bypass. This is a vulnerability-surface enumeration query, not a confirmed compromise. Rationale: Article: 'If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you're automatically vulnerable to a BitLocker bypass.' This isn't malicious by itself, so it ships as hunting tier to enumerate the vulnerable population and pre-stage incident response. The query keys on MpCmdRun.exe -OfflineScan which is the only documented way the offline scan feature is invoked.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1542.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • End user clicking 'Microsoft Defender Offline scan' in Windows Security to clean a malware infection
  • Helpdesk-triggered offline scan as part of a documented remediation playbook
  • EDR/AV testing in a lab where analysts exercise the offline-scan flow
  • Managed IT scripts that automate periodic offline scans on kiosks
  • Vendor support sessions guiding a user through Defender troubleshooting
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and parent process — was this a UI-driven Security Center action (legitimate-shaped) or a scripted invocation (suspicious)? 2) Contain: do not action a single hit; instead tag the host as 'GreatXML-vulnerable' in the asset inventory and re-verify ReAgent.xml integrity on that host's recovery partition. 3) Hunt: within 24h of each hit, search the same DeviceId for the UC1 file-write signature, shutdown.exe /r /o, and reagentc.exe modifications — those three together with this prerequisite constitute the full GreatXML kill chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "MpCmdRun.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-OfflineScan", "OfflineScan", "-BootSafeMode")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          IntegrityLevel = ProcessIntegrityLevel
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            Hits = count(), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 5)
            by DeviceName, AccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\MpCmdRun.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("-OfflineScan", "OfflineScan", "-BootSafeMode")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(), Cmds = make_set(CommandLine, 5)
          by Computer, Account
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Microsoft Defender Offline Scan Initiation (GreatXML Prerequisite)

description: Microsoft Defender Offline Scan being initiated via MpCmdRun.exe puts the host into the GreatXML-vulnerable WinRE state. Hunt only, since the feature is legitimate.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Reagentc.exe reconfiguring WinRE image path or enabling recovery boot AIInstallation Medium
Detects use of the Windows reagentc.exe utility to relocate, re-enable, or set the WinRE image — operations that directly manipulate the surface the GreatXML exploit abuses, and that are uncommon outside servicing windows. Rationale: The GreatXML bypass requires a manipulated WinRE image to be in place; reagentc.exe is the supported way to register or relocate that image. Filtering out servicing-stack parents (TiWorker, TrustedInstaller) keeps Windows Update reconfigurations quiet while leaving interactive/scripted abuse visible. The /boottore flag in particular forces the next reboot into WinRE — a giveaway of the exploit sequence.
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1574
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT administrator manually re-registering WinRE after a failed feature update ('reagentc /setreimage')
  • Vendor OEM imaging script setting /setosimage during build
  • Engineering bench scripts that toggle /enable + /disable for WinRE testing
  • Helpdesk recovery troubleshooting flagged in the change ticketing system
  • Endpoint configuration baseline tools (e.g. some MDM agents) calling reagentc /enable on first boot
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sfc" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is in an active patching / feature-update window in WSUS/Intune. Check the cmdline for '/setreimage <path>' and confirm the path points to a normal C:\Windows\System32\Recovery location vs. a user-writable directory. 2) Contain: if outside a change window, isolate the host and dump the current ReAgentConfig (reagentc /info) plus the recovery partition contents before reboot. Disable WinRE temporarily on critical assets via reagentc /disable until staged content is reviewed. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same DeviceId for the UC1 file-write signature and for any shutdown.exe /r /o that would actually trigger the bypass.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "reagentc.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/setreimage", "/enable", "/boottore", "/setosimage")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe", "WindowsUpdateBox.exe", "setupcl.exe", "DismHost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandParent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          IntegrityLevel = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          IsRemoteSession = AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\reagentc.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/setreimage", "/enable", "/boottore", "/setosimage")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\TiWorker.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\TrustedInstaller.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\WindowsUpdateBox.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Reagentc.exe Reconfiguring WinRE Image or Recovery Boot (GreatXML Exploit Path)

description: reagentc.exe is the supported tool for managing the WinRE image and recovery-boot state. Outside of OS servicing it is rarely invoked, and the GreatXML bypass depends on a manipulable WinRE image — flag interactive use.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:

logsource:

| ImageFileName=/\\reagentc\.exe$/i

| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/(TiWorker|TrustedInstaller|WindowsUpdateBox|DismHost)\.exe$/i

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="reagentc.exe" AND (Processes.process="*/setreimage*" OR Processes.process="*/enable*" OR Processes.process="*/boottore*" OR Processes.process="*/setosimage*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Reboot to WinRE via shutdown /r /o (GreatXML exploit trigger) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the final trigger of the GreatXML chain — a user-mode invocation of shutdown.exe with the /o (Advanced Options) flag, which is the scripted equivalent of holding Shift while clicking Restart and is what actually boots the host into the manipulated WinRE. Rationale: The article explicitly instructs the attacker to 'Reboot to WinRE by holding Shift while clicking Restart.' The non-GUI equivalent of that exact action is shutdown.exe /r /o — the only documented combination of switches that triggers a reboot into the Advanced Boot Options / WinRE menu. Pairing /r with /o eliminates almost all benign reboot noise.
ATT&CKT1529 T1542.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk script that boots a user into Advanced Options for safe-mode troubleshooting
  • Engineering driver-signing or kernel-debug workflow that repeatedly enters WinRE
  • Build-lab automation that toggles secure-boot / test-signing modes
  • End user who learned about shutdown.exe flags from a tutorial
  • Microsoft Endpoint Manager remediation script that uses shutdown /r /o for advanced recovery
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "intunemanagementextension.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "FastBoot"
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the shutdown event with the immediately preceding 24h on the same DeviceId for UC1 (XML file writes), UC2 (offline-scan initiation), or UC3 (reagentc reconfig). A standalone /r /o is low-value; chained with the other UCs it is high-value. 2) Contain: pre-emptively re-seal BitLocker (suspend + resume protectors, rotate the recovery key) on any host that exhibits the chain — assume the recovery key is compromised. 3) Hunt: post-reboot, inspect the host on next agent check-in for anomalous file writes against C:\ at SYSTEM integrity that lack a parent process (a typical artifact of operations performed from WinRE while the EDR agent was offline).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "shutdown.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/o\b"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/r\b"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandParent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          IsRemoteSession = AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

title: Shutdown to Advanced Boot Options / WinRE via shutdown.exe /r /o
id: 12af48d6-3e07-49aa-a31c-77b8ce410f9d
description: shutdown.exe invoked with both /r and /o forces a reboot into the Windows Recovery / Advanced Boot Options menu — the trigger step of the GreatXML BitLocker bypass and equivalent to the article's Shift+Restart instruction.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
    - attack.defense_evasion
    - attack.t1529
    - attack.t1542.003
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith: '\shutdown.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: ' /o'
    selection_reboot:
        CommandLine|contains: ' /r'
    condition: selection and selection_reboot
falsepositives:
    - IT helpdesk guiding a user into Advanced Boot Options for legitimate troubleshooting
    - Engineering / driver-development workflows requiring repeated WinRE entry
level: medium

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\shutdown.exe OR *\\Shutdown.exe OR *\\SHUTDOWN.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\ \/o* OR *\ \/O*) @CommandLine:(*\ \/r* OR *\ \/R*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\shutdown\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\s\/o\b/i
| CommandLine=/\s\/r\b/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=firstSeen)])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="shutdown.exe" Processes.process="*/o*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| eval has_r=if(match(process,"(?i)\\s/r\\b"),1,0), has_o=if(match(process,"(?i)\\s/o\\b"),1,0)
| where has_r=1 AND has_o=1
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="shutdown.exe" Processes.process="*/o*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| eval has_r=if(match(process,"(?i)\\s/r\\b"),1,0), has_o=if(match(process,"(?i)\\s/o\\b"),1,0)
| where has_r=1 AND has_o=1
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45585")

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45585")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Critical
